column2: In SQL Server, SUM(Amount) {{c1::OVER}} (PARTITION BY CustomerID) calculates a total alongside each customer's rows.
column3:
OVER makes the aggregate keep individual rows instead of collapsing them into groups.
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount,
       SUM(Amount) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID) AS CustomerTotal
FROM dbo.Orders;
Review source

column2: To total Amount separately per customer, use SUM(Amount) OVER ({{c1::PARTITION BY CustomerID}}).
column3:
The same customer's total can repeat on each of that customer's orders. Other customers' amounts are excluded from that calculation.
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount,
       SUM(Amount) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID) AS CustomerTotal
FROM dbo.Orders;
Review source

column2: With unique ProductID, ROW_NUMBER() OVER ({{c1::ORDER BY Price DESC, ProductID}}) numbers highest prices first and breaks ties by ProductID.
column3:
The price sets the main ordering and ProductID resolves ties. This window order does not sort the returned result by itself.
SELECT ProductID, Price,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Price DESC, ProductID) AS RowNum
FROM dbo.Product; -- ProductID is unique
Review source

column2: For SQL Server SUM with window ORDER BY but no explicit frame, the default is {{c1::RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW}}.
column3:
RANGE extends the frame through peers tied on the sort keys. Use ROWS when you want the frame to end at the current position.
SELECT Price, Amount,
       SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS RangeTotal
FROM (VALUES (10, 5), (10, 7), (20, 3)) AS t(Price, Amount)
ORDER BY Price; -- Both Price 10 rows have RangeTotal 12.
Review source

column2: To divide products into four roughly equal-sized price groups, use {{c1::NTILE(4)}} OVER (ORDER BY Price DESC).
column3:
NTILE divides by row positions, not distinct price values. A tie can therefore fall on both sides of a group boundary.
SELECT ProductID, Price,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY Price DESC, ProductID) AS PriceGroup
FROM dbo.Product; -- ProductID is unique
Review source

column2: With unique OrderID, a row-by-row running total uses SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID {{c1::ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW}}).
column3:
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING starts at the first row in the partition. CURRENT ROW ends at the current row's position.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS RunningTotal
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID; -- Running totals: 10, 30, 60
Review source

column2: With unique OrderID, AVG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID ROWS BETWEEN {{c1::2 PRECEDING}} AND CURRENT ROW) averages up to three orders.
column3:
The frame uses the available positions at the start. The second row can average only two values.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       AVG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID
           ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS MovingAverage
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: A frame covering the current row and up to two following rows uses ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND {{c1::2 FOLLOWING}}.
column3:
The frame stops early if it reaches the end of the partition. It does not pull rows from the next partition.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID
           ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 2 FOLLOWING) AS ForwardTotal
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: When omitted, the row offset for LAG and LEAD defaults to {{c1::1}}.
column3:
LAG reads backward and LEAD reads forward by that number. The window ordering defines the previous and next positions.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       LAG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS PreviousAmount,
       LEAD(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS NextAmount
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: On a partition's first row, LAG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) returns {{c1::NULL}}.
column3:
No prior row exists in this partition. An explicitly supplied default would let you choose a different value.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       LAG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS PreviousAmount
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: With unique OrderID, change from the previous amount uses Amount - {{c1::LAG(Amount,1,0)}} OVER (ORDER BY OrderID).
column3:
When a previous row exists, its amount is subtracted. Zero applies only when that requested row is absent.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       Amount - LAG(Amount, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS Change
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: To read Amount two rows ahead, use LEAD(Amount,{{c1::2}},0) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID).
column3:
The offset counts ahead in window order. Near the partition end, zero supplies the value for a missing second following row.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       LEAD(Amount, 2, 0) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS TwoAhead
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: With unique OrderID and default NULL handling, {{c1::FIRST_VALUE(Amount)}} OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) returns the first ordered Amount.
column3:
The first ordered row supplies the value even if its Amount is NULL. It is not necessarily the smallest Amount.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       FIRST_VALUE(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS FirstAmount,
       LAST_VALUE(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS LastAmount
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: With unique OrderID, LAST_VALUE(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID {{c1::ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING}}) reaches the partition's final row.
column3:
The upper frame boundary reaches the final ordered row for every result row. The default frame can stop much earlier.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       FIRST_VALUE(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS FirstAmount,
       LAST_VALUE(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS LastAmount
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source

column2: The first row of any SQL Server PERCENT_RANK partition has a result of {{c1::0}}.
column3:
The first rank contributes zero in the relative-rank calculation. Ties at that rank receive the same result.
SELECT Price,
       PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS RelativeRank,
       CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS CumulativeDistribution
FROM (VALUES (10), (20), (20)) AS p(Price)
ORDER BY Price;
Review source

column2: For one partition containing ascending values 10,20,20, CUME_DIST() gives both 20 rows {{c1::1.0}}.
column3:
For each 20, the count includes the other 20 as a peer. Both divide three qualifying values by three total values.
SELECT Price,
       PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS RelativeRank,
       CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS CumulativeDistribution
FROM (VALUES (10), (20), (20)) AS p(Price)
ORDER BY Price;
Review source

column2: SQL Server ranking functions reject {{c1::ROWS and RANGE}} frame clauses.
column3:
An aggregate can define a frame, but a ranking function uses the ordered partition without one.
Review source

column2: In LAG(Amount,1,0), the final argument supplies {{c1::the value for a missing preceding row}}.
column3:
If the preceding row exists and its Amount is NULL, LAG returns that NULL under default NULL handling.
SELECT OrderID, Amount,
       LAG(Amount, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY OrderID) AS PreviousAmount
FROM (VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30)) AS o(OrderID, Amount)
ORDER BY OrderID;
Review source
